title: India's Software Exports Jump 8.2% to $221.4 Billion as US Share Grows
excerpt: The RBI's annual survey shows American clients now account for 54.1% of exports, with total receipts including overseas operations hitting $239.3 billion.
body:
• India's software services exports rose 8.2% to $221.4 billion in 2025-26, excluding sales through overseas commercial presence, according to the RBI's annual survey released September 18.
  • Including the overseas operations of Indian firms, total software export receipts reached $239.3 billion, up 9.5% year-on-year.
  • The US remained the dominant destination at 54.1% of exports — $119.7 billion, up 11% — while Europe accounted for 31.8%, with the UK at 15.4%.
  • IT services led at $147 billion, but software product development exports slipped to $6.4 billion from $6.8 billion, and off-site delivery from India made up 91.7% of all exports.

India's software exports accelerated in the year ended March 2026, rising 8.2% to $221.4 billion as American demand for Indian technology services deepened, the Reserve Bank of India's annual survey showed on Friday.

The numbers

The RBI's Survey on Computer Software and Information Technology Enabled Services Exports: 2025-26 showed exports excluding sales through the overseas commercial presence of Indian companies climbing from $204.7 billion in 2024-25 to $221.4 billion. The growth rate improved on the 7.3% recorded the previous year. The survey drew responses from 2,363 operating entities out of 7,569 exporters contacted, representing roughly 89% of the country's software export ecosystem.

When services supplied through the overseas commercial presence of Indian companies are included, total software services exports reached $239.3 billion in 2025-26, up 9.5% from $218.6 billion a year earlier. Local software business conducted by foreign affiliates increased to $17.9 billion from $13.9 billion, with the US the largest market for those overseas operations, followed by the UK.

America deepens its share

The United States retained its position as India's largest client by a wide margin. Aggregate export billings to the US rose 11% to $119.7 billion, lifting the American share of total software exports to 54.1%. Europe formed the second-largest destination with a 31.8% share, within which the United Kingdom accounted for 15.4% of total exports.

The remote-first model remains the industry's defining feature: off-site delivery, where services are provided remotely from India, constituted 91.7% of all software services exports in 2025-26.

The US dollar continued to dominate invoicing. Exports billed in dollars increased to $160.7 billion from $147.4 billion, taking the dollar's share to 72.6% from 72%. The euro remained the second-largest invoicing currency at 9.6%, while the rupee's share declined to 6.3% from 7.1% and the pound sterling held about 6%.

What India sells

Computer services remained the largest component, accounting for 69.3% of total software services exports, up from 67.4% a year earlier. Within computer services, IT services exports rose to $147 billion from $131.3 billion, while software product development exports declined to $6.4 billion from $6.8 billion — its share slipping to 2.9% from 3.3%.

IT-enabled services exports increased to $68 billion from $66.6 billion. Business process outsourcing continued to dominate ITES, accounting for $56 billion, or 82.4%, led by specialized workflows in finance, taxation consulting, bookkeeping and accounting. Engineering services contributed $12 billion, up from $10.8 billion.

Private limited companies remained the industry's backbone: their exports increased 9.3% to $134.6 billion, taking their share to 60.8% from 60.1%. Public limited companies recorded exports of $81.7 billion, up from $77.2 billion.

Why it matters

The acceleration matters beyond the industry. Software services are the engine of India's services surplus and a core support for the current account. A deepening US concentration — 54.1% and climbing — ties the sector's fortunes tightly to American corporate technology spending and, by extension, to US immigration and outsourcing policy. The weakness in software product development, now a second straight area of softness, is the one blemish on an otherwise broad-based report.

Diaspora angle

For Indian professionals in the US technology sector, the numbers confirm what hiring patterns already show: American enterprise demand is the single biggest driver of Indian IT growth. Investors with exposure to Indian IT — directly or through index funds — are effectively holding a leveraged bet on US corporate IT budgets.

What's next

The industry will watch whether momentum holds into FY2026-27 as artificial intelligence-led transformation reshapes how clients buy technology services. The questions to track: whether IT services growth survives the shift from traditional outsourcing to AI-assisted delivery, whether the product-development slump reverses, and whether the rupee can regain any share as an invoicing currency.
